strengths: Originality/significance: The integration of CAD-based segmentation, 6D pose estimation, failure detection, and automatic re-localization addresses a practically important deployment problem. Treating tracking failure as a learned classification task is a useful systems idea, although the components are individually incremental.

Soundness: The reported results are promising: SOM obtains 68.5 mean mAP across five BOP datasets, and the full system improves over FoundationPose tracking on the modified YCB-Video evaluation. Comparisons to ground-truth-mask FoundationPose also help identify segmentation as a principal performance bottleneck.

Presentation: The two-module SOM/TOM decomposition and overall execution flow are understandable, and the main figures provide helpful qualitative illustrations of segmentation, pose estimation, and recovery.
Analysis: The manuscript includes ablations for language injection, HSFA depth, DINOv2 fine-tuning, and attention in the tracking classifier, as well as latency measurements.
Ethics: The work concerns standard object pose estimation benchmarks and does not present an evident major ethical risk.
weaknesses: Soundness: The central claim that SOM is label-free or self-supervised is contradicted by the methodology. Equation 2 explicitly optimizes pixel predictions against ground-truth labels, and Appendix D states that every query image has a corresponding mask used in synchronized augmentation. The paper neither explains where these masks originate nor defines a self-supervised procedure for producing them. This makes the supervision regime—and consequently the headline comparison against supervised and unsupervised methods—unreliable.

Soundness: The tracking evidence does not substantiate claims about robust recovery from severe real-world occlusion and rapid motion. Evaluation is limited to YCB-Video modified with unspecified random frame dropping and random masks. Negatives are largely different-object pairs or random/shifted crops, which may make classification much easier than detecting realistic tracker drift. There are no results on natural track-loss sequences, disappearance and re-entry, false re-initialization rates, failure-detection precision/recall, recovery time, or performance as occlusion and motion severity vary.

Evaluation: The claimed state of the art is insufficiently supported. Pose estimation is compared only with FoundationPose using CNOS or ground-truth masks, despite the text describing a different DINO/SAM2 baseline; relevant CAD-based methods such as SAM-6D are not compared end-to-end. Table 2 mixes supervision categories and leaderboard packages without enough protocol, version, or hardware information to establish comparability. No sample counts, repeated trials, confidence intervals, or significance analysis are reported.

Evaluation leakage: Appendix E states that AP on the test set was measured every 1,000 steps, and the reported architectural choice was informed by these test results. This compromises the independence of the test evaluation. The manuscript also trains on subsets of the same BOP datasets and object inventories used for testing, so claims of zero-shot generalization to novel objects require a clearly documented instance-disjoint protocol that is currently absent.

Reproducibility: Core specifications are missing, including feature and attention dimensions, numbers of heads, input resolution, prompt text, mask-generation procedure, train/validation/test splits, decision threshold, memory-pool policy, rendering settings, modified-YCB evaluation parameters, and baseline configurations. The abstract promises open-source code and the paper contains a blank “Code:” field, but no repository or artifact is supplied.

Reproducibility is further undermined by major internal contradictions: the main text specifies AdamW while Appendix D specifies SGD for SOM; Equation 2 uses Tversky plus focal loss with weights 1.0 and 0.2, whereas the appendix specifies focal, Dice, IoU, and Tversky losses with substantially different weights and parameters; TOM is trained for 15 epochs with AdamW in the main text but 10 epochs with Adam in the appendix; and the hardware description conflicts with the reported eight-A100 training setup.

Presentation: Several claims are overstated or inconsistent. The system is called annotation-free despite its apparent use of training masks and BOP ground-truth masks for TOM; “real time” is asserted without a full-pipeline throughput analysis, including costly re-registration and LLM processing; SOM runtime is reported as 0.183 s in Table 2 but 0.265 s with language in Table 5; and the paper alternates between cosine-threshold failure detection and a learned classifier without clearly specifying the deployed rule. Numerous grammatical and typographical errors further impede precision.

Limitations: There is no substantive limitations discussion covering dependence on accurate textured CAD models, domain shift between rendering and observations, visually similar distractors, symmetric objects, LLM prompt variability, memory growth, compute requirements, or failure-detector errors. The ethical risk is low, but dataset licensing, release details for the claimed new tracking dataset, and possible privacy considerations for future real-world video deployment are not addressed.

strengths: Significance: The manuscript addresses a practically important problem—automatic initialization and recovery for model-based 6D object tracking—where reducing manual-mask requirements could materially simplify robotics deployment.

Methodological concept: Combining CAD renderings, DINOv2/CLIP features, prompted segmentation, FoundationPose, and failure-triggered re-registration forms a coherent end-to-end system. The memory-based recovery mechanism is intuitively useful.

Evaluation breadth: SOM is evaluated across five BOP datasets, while the paper reports pose, segmentation, tracking, runtime, and several component ablations. The reported numbers, if established under a valid common protocol, would be promising.

Presentation: The high-level pipeline and the roles of SOM, TOM, and HSFA are understandable from Figures 2–4, and the appendix attempts to document metrics, augmentation, and training. weaknesses: Soundness—supervision contradiction: The central claim that SOM is “self-supervised,” “label-free,” and trained using “exclusively unlabeled RGB frames” is incompatible with the method. Equations 2–3 require pixel targets, Appendix D says each query image has a “corresponding mask” transformed jointly with it, and the reported focal/Dice/IoU/Tversky losses all require masks. The manuscript never explains how these training masks are obtained without annotations. TOM explicitly uses BOP ground-truth masks. Consequently, the headline annotation-free comparison against supervised and unsupervised methods is not substantiated.

Soundness—evaluation protocol: SOM is trained on subsets of the same named datasets used for testing, including LMO, YCB-V, HB, T-LESS, and TUD-L. Although separate benchmark splits may have been used, the paper does not specify image, scene, or object-level separation, nor whether masks or instances overlap. This prevents assessing the claimed zero-shot generalization and raises serious leakage concerns.

Soundness—tracking evidence: Recovery is evaluated only by synthetically dropping frames and masking YCB-V objects. The construction, corruption severity, random seeds, split, and overlap with TOM training data are unspecified. Table 4 reports only accuracy on an apparently balanced synthetic pair dataset, without precision/recall, AUROC, threshold selection, per-object generalization, or false-trigger rates. Table 3 compares recovery-enabled STORM to FoundationPose tracking without a comparable re-detection mechanism, so it does not isolate classifier quality or establish superiority over existing recovery strategies.

Soundness—metrics and claims: Table 1 labels quantities “Mean ADD” and “Mean ADD-S,” treats larger values as better, and reports them like recalls, whereas Appendix B defines ADD/ADD-S as distances for which lower is better. Thresholds and aggregation are missing. Table 2 mixes methods from different supervision regimes and largely uncited leaderboard executables without documenting versions, inputs, hardware, or a verified common evaluation protocol. There are no uncertainty estimates or repeated runs despite small reported differences.

Reproducibility: Major specifications conflict. The main text says SOM uses AdamW, whereas Appendix D says SGD; the main loss is Tversky plus focal with weights 1.0/0.2 and Tversky parameters 0.3/0.7, whereas the appendix uses focal, Dice, IoU, and Tversky with different weights and parameters; TOM is trained for 15 epochs in Section 4 but 10 epochs in Appendix D. The paper also omits attention dimensions, segmentation-model choice/configuration, failure threshold, memory size/update policy, rendering details, data counts for SOM, seeds, and exact benchmark commands. It promises open-source code/data, but the manuscript supplies no repository or artifact link.

Originality: HSFA appears to be a relatively standard sequence of self-attention, cross-attention, text conditioning, and upsampling, while TOM is a one-layer attention binary matcher wrapped around FoundationPose. The manuscript does not provide sufficient formal or empirical comparison against closely related feature-fusion, tracking-confidence, or re-detection designs to establish substantial methodological novelty.

Significance and runtime: The practical premise is valuable, but the evidence does not support “real-time” operation. Reported SOM latency of 0.183 s is about 5.5 fps; TOM plus FoundationPose is approximately 98 ms per frame, about 10 fps; and the language-enabled ablation reports 0.265 s. End-to-end latency, re-registration cost, rendering/preprocessing time, hardware-normalized comparisons, and throughput under repeated failures are absent.

Presentation and limitations: The paper contains malformed text (“Code:” with no link), inconsistent terminology and baselines (DINO-based versus CNOS in the Q1 description/table), typographical issues, and low-resolution ablation plots. It lacks a substantive limitations discussion addressing synthetic tracking failures, single-object scope, dependence on textured CAD renderings and large pretrained models, domain shift, compute cost, and false recovery triggers.

Research ethics/data governance: No major inherent ethical hazard is apparent, but the custom tracking dataset’s release terms, source-dataset licensing, privacy review, and construction documentation are not discussed. Given the central dataset and reproducibility claims, these omissions should be resolved. Overall, the numerous contradictions and insufficient controls make the headline results unreliable in their present form.

strengths: Significance: STORM addresses a practically important problem by unifying automatic object segmentation, 6D pose estimation, tracking-failure detection, and re-localization from a supplied 3D model. Automatic recovery after occlusion or rapid motion could substantially reduce deployment effort in robotics.

Soundness: The reported results are promising. SOM obtains 68.5 mean mAP across five BOP datasets, exceeding the listed alternatives, while STORM improves over FoundationPose+CNOS on LM-O and YCB-Video. TOM also raises YCB-Video tracking AR from 50.09 to 67.85 with modest reported overhead.

Originality: Hierarchical Spatial Fusion Attention combines rendered multi-view, query-image, and language features in a coherent way, while the learned failure detector and memory-triggered re-registration form a useful system-level contribution.

The evaluation covers varied BOP datasets containing textured, textureless, symmetric, and occluded objects. Ablations examine language injection, HSFA depth, DINOv2 fine-tuning, and the attention-based TOM classifier.
Presentation: The high-level pipeline and motivation are generally understandable, and the main architecture diagram clearly separates segmentation and tracking stages.
The application raises no obvious human-subject or data-privacy concerns, and the stated intention to release code and the tracking dataset would benefit reproducibility.
weaknesses: Soundness: The central annotation-free/self-supervised claim is not adequately supported. The segmentation objective requires target masks, and Appendix D explicitly augments each query image together with its “corresponding mask,” yet the manuscript never explains how these masks are obtained without annotations. TOM explicitly uses BOP ground-truth masks. This unresolved issue directly affects the claimed supervision setting and the fairness of Table 2.

The training and evaluation protocol does not establish the claimed zero-shot generalization. SOM is trained on subsets of LMO, YCBV, HB, TLESS, and TUDL—the same datasets used for testing—but no image-, scene-, or object-level split is specified. It is therefore unclear whether test objects or closely related observations appear during training.

The pose metrics are inconsistently defined. Tables treat larger ADD and ADD-S values as better, apparently reporting thresholded recall, whereas Appendix B defines ADD/ADD-S as distances for which lower is better. Threshold aggregation and averaging are not fully specified, making the headline pose results difficult to reproduce or compare.

Evidence for robust re-localization is limited. The tracking evaluation modifies only YCB-Video using unspecified random frame dropping and masking, reports no corruption severities, split, uncertainty, or repeated trials, and compares primarily against FoundationPose without evaluating other recovery/re-detection strategies. Table 4 measures synthetic-pair classification accuracy rather than end-to-end recovery precision, recall, false-trigger rate, or time-to-recovery.

Several experimental descriptions conflict: the main text says SOM uses AdamW, while Appendix D says SGD; TOM is described as trained for 15 epochs in the main text but 10 epochs in the appendix; and the main loss contains only Tversky and focal terms while the appendix lists focal, Dice, IoU, and Tversky losses with different weights. These contradictions materially impair reproducibility.

The “real-time” claim is insufficiently justified. SOM alone takes 0.183–0.265 seconds per image, and the paper does not clearly report end-to-end latency including language generation, rendering, segmentation, registration, tracking, and re-registration. Baseline runtimes also are not shown to use identical hardware and settings.

Originality is somewhat incremental: the system largely composes DINOv2, CLIP/Gemma, SAM2, and FoundationPose with attention-based fusion and a binary verification head. Stronger component-matched baselines are needed to isolate the benefit of HSFA from additional training, semantic conditioning, and overall system composition.

Presentation contains consequential inconsistencies: the Q1 baseline is described as a DINOv2+SAM2 pipeline but Table 1 lists CNOS; “self-supervised,” “unsupervised,” “zero-shot,” and “annotation-free” are used without precise definitions; and the overall mAP equation omits normalization by the number of datasets.

Reproducibility currently depends on a promised release. Important details remain absent, including dataset splits, mask provenance, failure thresholds, memory-pool update policy and capacity, corruption parameters, random seeds, confidence intervals, and full end-to-end evaluation code.

Limitations are treated mainly as future work rather than analyzed directly. The manuscript should discuss dependence on an accurate textured 3D model and large pretrained components, failure modes for visually similar instances and severe/long occlusions, sensitivity to synthetic-to-real mismatch, and the safety implications of false recovery in robotic deployment. These issues prevent the current evidence from reliably supporting the paper’s strongest claims.

strengths: Soundness: The modular pipeline is sensible: reference-conditioned segmentation, FoundationPose-based registration/tracking, and explicit failure-triggered re-localization address complementary failure modes. Controlled comparisons keep the downstream pose estimator fixed, and the paper reports five-run variation for its principal results.

Presentation: The manuscript is generally clear and well organized. It explicitly distinguishes frozen components from trainable SOM/TOM modules, gives equations for HSFA conditioning and TOM thresholding, and includes useful runtime and component ablations.

Significance: Automatic failure detection and recovery could be practically valuable for robotic pose tracking. The reported improvements over FoundationPose+CNOS on LM-O/YCB-V and over unverified FoundationPose tracking on corrupted YCB-V are substantial.

The limitations section appropriately clarifies that 'zero-shot' means annotation- and adaptation-free inference rather than category-disjoint novel-object generalization, and acknowledges dependencies on SAM3D, FoundationPose, threshold calibration, and object properties.
The paper provides hardware, optimization, augmentation, loss, reference-count, and latency information, and evaluates segmentation across five BOP datasets.
weaknesses: Soundness: The evidence does not establish the central CAD-free, single-image 6D-pose claim. BOP training and testing contain the same object identities, training uses rendered views from available CAD models, and the manuscript does not clearly state whether the single reference used for Table 2 is a real image, a CAD rendering, or a reconstruction rendering. Thus these results do not demonstrate generalization to a new object supplied only as one photograph.

The SAM3D evaluation uses the corresponding ground-truth CAD mesh to estimate a similarity alignment before pose evaluation. This leaks precisely the benchmark scale and coordinate frame unavailable in the claimed CAD-free deployment. A single uncalibrated image cannot generally determine metric object scale, and no CAD-free metric-scale or robotic evaluation resolves this issue. Consequently, Table 3 cannot support the practical claim that reconstructed geometry replaces curated CAD assets.

The tracking evidence is too narrow for the robustness claims. Table 4 uses only a mildly modified YCB-V setting: perturbations occur with probability 0.1, occluders cover only 10-20% of the object bounding-box area, and motion is simulated by independent frame dropping. This does not substantiate claims about severe occlusion, rapid viewpoint changes, or broad real-world recovery.

TOM is trained and primarily evaluated on synthetic pair corruptions generated from BOP annotations, including random crop shifts and identity swaps. Such negatives may be much easier and systematically different from genuine FoundationPose failure trajectories. The only closed-loop comparison is against unmodified FoundationPose; there are no learned-confidence, similarity-threshold, detector/re-initialization, or contemporary video-tracking recovery baselines.

The segmentation comparison is difficult to interpret fairly: several baselines are unnamed leaderboard packages without publications, runtime numbers come from heterogeneous systems, and supervised versus adaptation-free groupings do not control training data or access to target identities. Calling the result state of the art is therefore insufficiently supported.

Originality is modest. HSFA is principally a composition of standard self-attention, cross-attention, and FiLM/AdaLN conditioning. TOM is a BCE compatibility classifier whose negative logit is renamed an energy-like score and combined with conventional EMA, thresholding, and persistence. The system integration may be useful, but the individual methodological ideas are incremental.

Reproducibility is inadequate despite some implementation detail. The code link is blank, and the paper omits exact DINOv3, CLIP, VLM, and SAM3D checkpoints; major architectural dimensions and memory aggregation details; SOM training duration; TOM train/validation/test splits; the calibrated threshold value; and sufficient information to reproduce several leaderboard baselines.

Some empirical statements are inaccurate or unclear: Table 1 does not exactly match the ground-truth-mask setting on YCB-V as claimed, Table 8 reports roughly 95% AP without clearly defining the test set or reconciling it with the 67.7 BOP mean AP, and average runtime appears to exclude or inadequately account for expensive reconstruction, registration, and recovery events.

Significance is consequently limited by reliance on large frozen proprietary/recent foundation components, eight-A100 training, identity-overlapping benchmark data, and no category-disjoint, real-robot, multi-object, transparent, reflective, or thin-object evaluation.

Research ethics are not a decisive concern, but the impact statement is cursory for a physical-AI system: it does not discuss physical safety under false verifier decisions, surveillance or dual-use applications, or biases inherited from the VLM and foundation-model components.

The manuscript is generally readable and clearly separates inherited frozen components from the trainable SOM/HSFA and TOM modules. It reports segmentation, pose, verification, recovery, ablation, and runtime results rather than relying on a single metric.
The reference-count study, language-conditioning ablation, attention-depth experiments, five-seed variation for the proposed system, and component-level H100 timings are useful diagnostic efforts.

The limitations section commendably clarifies that “zero-shot” means annotation- and adaptation-free inference rather than category-disjoint novel-object generalization, and acknowledges dependence on reconstruction quality, FoundationPose, and threshold calibration.
weaknesses: The central CAD-free, single-image 6D-pose claim is not convincingly supported. Table 1 changes only the mask source while holding FoundationPose fixed, but does not establish that the reported pose results use a reconstruction obtained without benchmark CAD information. In Table 3, the successful SAM3D condition is aligned to the ground-truth CAD mesh through similarity ICP, including scale, rotation, and translation. This supplies exactly the metric scale and coordinate alignment that monocular reconstruction cannot generally determine. The assertion that deployment can simply use a self-consistent reconstructed frame does not resolve metric scale or robot-frame pose, so the principal deployment claim remains unvalidated.

The claimed generalization setting is weak. SOM is trained on the training splits of LM/LM-O, T-LESS, TUD-L, HB, and YCB-V and then evaluated on test scenes containing the same benchmark identities. Thus “annotation-free” applies only at inference, while the model has received supervised masks and identity-specific appearances for the evaluated object universe. Comparisons against methods labeled supervised, and statements about zero-shot generalization, are consequently easy to misinterpret and do not demonstrate novel-object performance.

The tracking evidence is largely synthetic and does not establish real failure detection. TOM is trained from ground-truth masked crops, shifted/random negatives, and identity swaps, then evaluated using artificial YCB-V corruptions constructed with ground-truth object masks and boxes. The main stress setting is mild—10% frame-drop probability and 10% probability of masking only 10–20% of the bounding-box area—and it is unclear whether identities or sequences are disjoint across TOM training, calibration, and evaluation. There is no evaluation on naturally occurring labeled failures, category-disjoint objects, real camera motion, or robotic operation.

The recovery comparison is not controlled fairly. STORM combines FoundationPose with a learned failure detector and re-localization, whereas the baseline is bare FoundationPose tracking, which by construction cannot reset. Missing comparisons include periodic re-localization, confidence-based heuristics, alternative learned verifiers, an oracle detector, and a common re-localization policy. Detection delay, false-alarm rate, number of recoveries, recovery success rate, and pose accuracy conditional on corruption severity are also absent.

Several inconsistencies reduce confidence in the results. The text says STORM “matches the ground-truth setup exactly” on YCB-V although Table 1 reports 77/98/73 versus 78/99/74. Table 8 reports 94.6–95.4 AP under an unspecified “same BOP training protocol,” far above the 67.7 aggregate in Tables 2 and 7, without identifying the evaluated dataset or explaining the discrepancy. AP, mAP, AP_C, and “mean AP” are used ambiguously. Baseline runtimes appear to come from heterogeneous leaderboard systems, with no evidence of identical hardware or implementations.

The methodological originality is modest. HSFA is a composition of self-attention, cross-attention, FiLM/AdaLN conditioning, and a decoder; TOM is a BCE-trained pair classifier followed by EMA thresholding and a consecutive-frame rule. Calling the negative BCE logit an “energy-like” score is only a monotonic sign change and provides no energy-based training or calibration guarantee. The empirical study does not compare against sufficiently strong learned reference-fusion, video-segmentation, uncertainty-estimation, or tracking-verification alternatives to isolate a substantive conceptual advance.

Reproducibility is inadequate for the reported contribution. The code link is blank. Important details are missing, including exact DINOv3, CLIP, VLM, SAM3D, and FoundationPose variants/checkpoints; SOM layer dimensions and positional encoding; training duration and warm-up schedule; precise train/validation/test partitions; the calibrated threshold value; sequence and instance counts; corruption seeds; reference selection; and full end-to-end initialization/recovery latency. The claimed five independent runs are not sufficiently defined, especially for deterministic baselines and reconstruction.

The ablations do not adequately support the architectural claims. There is no controlled comparison against simple concatenation, cosine matching with an equivalent decoder, standard cross-attention, or other fusion modules. The language gain is only about 0.4 AP_C, without uncertainty or significance analysis in Table 7. TOM’s attention improvement is small in AUROC (95.6 to 96.4) despite a much larger accuracy change, suggesting threshold/class-balance sensitivity that is not analyzed.

The limitations discussion is honest but does not cure the evidential gaps: the same-identity evaluation, CAD-based alignment, synthetic failures, and absence of real deployment tests directly constrain the paper’s central claims rather than merely its reach. The impact statement is also too cursory for a system framed as improving safety in logistics and manufacturing; it does not discuss false-negative drift detection, unsafe re-localization, surveillance/dual-use concerns, or the need for independent safety mechanisms. These concerns do not alone create an ethical bar, but the claimed safety benefit is unsupported.

strengths: Soundness: The modular evaluation provides encouraging evidence: SOM substantially improves over CNOS on LM-O and YCB-V, the model-quality study isolates SAM3D geometry, and TOM improves the modified YCB-V tracking metrics over unmonitored FoundationPose. Several results include five-run variation and component ablations.

Significance: Explicitly detecting drift and triggering re-localization addresses a practical weakness of 6D pose trackers. The reported 9.1 ms TOM latency and roughly 25–33 FPS steady-state loop suggest potential real-time utility.

Originality: The combination of reference-query attention, optional language conditioning, reconstructed geometry, and learned tracking verification forms a coherent closed-loop system. The continuous compatibility signal is practically useful even though its ingredients are individually familiar.

Presentation: The manuscript is generally well organized, clearly distinguishes trainable from frozen components, provides algorithms and runtime profiles, and states that its “zero-shot” setting is not category-disjoint generalization. Ethics: The intended robotics applications and reliability motivation are reasonable, with no apparent use of sensitive human data or unresolved material ethical concern.
weaknesses: Soundness: The central “from a single image” and no-curated-CAD story is not convincingly demonstrated for metric 6D pose. The strong SAM3D result uses similarity alignment to the benchmark ground-truth CAD mesh, whereas the unaligned reconstruction performs dramatically worse (44.92 versus 99.12 ADD-S AUC). A single RGB image also leaves metric scale ambiguous. Saying that deployment only needs a self-consistent frame does not establish accurate metric translation or interoperability with a robot frame.

Soundness/generalization: SOM is trained on the BOP training splits containing the same object identities as the test splits. Thus the results do not establish novel-instance reference conditioning and cannot rule out identity memorization. Calling the method “annotation/adaptation-free” at inference is technically qualified in the paper, but the broad zero-shot framing and comparisons against generic reference-based systems overstate what is validated.

Evaluation: TOM is trained from synthetic same/different-object and randomly shifted crops, then tested mainly through mild synthetic YCB-V corruptions: frame dropping and 10–20% rectangular occlusion, each applied with probability 0.1. This does not substantiate claims of reliable recovery from severe occlusion or rapid real-world motion. There are no real failure annotations, category-disjoint sequences, clean-sequence degradation results, recovery latency/false-trigger analysis, or comparisons with alternative recovery mechanisms.

Evaluation: The end-to-end recovery comparison is only against FoundationPose without failure detection. Although Table 5 compares verifier architectures, it does not test whether a simple cosine or heuristic verifier coupled to the same EMA, persistence rule, and re-localization pipeline would yield similar pose recovery.

Originality: HSFA largely composes standard self-/cross-attention and FiLM-style language modulation, while TOM uses BCE classification followed by negated-logit thresholding, EMA smoothing, and a consecutive-frame rule. The main novelty is system integration rather than a substantial new learning principle.

Reproducibility: The stated code link is blank. Important specifications are missing or ambiguous, including exact DINOv3/CLIP/VLM variants, detailed layer dimensions, train/validation/test construction for TOM, numbers of training steps, checkpoint selection, and how the five evaluation seeds induce variation. This makes the headline results difficult to reproduce.

Presentation: Some claims exceed the evidence—for example, “state-of-the-art,” “strong generalization,” and recovery from “severe” failures. There are also minor inconsistencies, such as TOM latency differing between Tables 5 and 6 without an explicit hardware/protocol reconciliation, and several crowded or low-resolution figures.

Ethics/limitations: The limitations discussion is appropriately candid and should not be penalized, but the impact statement is too cursory for a physical-AI system; failure consequences and safeguards for safety-critical deployment deserve discussion. This is secondary to the evidential issues.
